title: Stop Weaponizing Jakob's Law
intro: Jakob's Law is about **prevalence** — patterns users meet constantly across the tools they actually use. One screenshot from a niche product is not evidence of a shared mental model.

learn.title: What the law actually says
learn.text:
Users spend most of their time on other sites, so they expect your site to work the way those sites work.

Any convention used on the **majority of products users interact with** gets burned into their mental models, and deviating from it creates friction.

In practical terms: don't reinvent the wheel.

try.q: What makes an appeal to Jakob's Law valid?
options: Users meet the pattern constantly, across many tools
A respected product uses the pattern
The pattern appears in a major design system
The team has used the pattern before without complaints
try.explain: The law is about prevalence across the user's whole digital environment.

left.label: Invalid use ✗
items: A niche example users rarely meet

right.label: Valid use ✓
items: Met daily across hundreds of apps

learn.title: The misuse pattern
learn.text:
**1.** A team introduces a novel interaction.
**2.** A usability concern is raised.
**3.** Someone finds a single screenshot from a niche tool doing something similar.
**4.** Jakob's Law is invoked and the discussion ends.

What's missing: any serious look at how often users actually encounter that pattern.

One team hid controls in a dense data table to look “cleaner”. When users couldn't find them in testing, a screenshot from one specialised tool was presented as proof.

try.q: Users fail to find hidden table controls, and a screenshot from one niche tool is offered as Jakob's Law proof. What is missing?
options: Evidence that users encounter that pattern often
A larger sample in the usability test
A second screenshot from another product
Agreement from the design system team
try.explain: Prevalence is the whole point of the law; one precedent isn't prevalence.

learn.title: The test before you invoke it
learn.text:
Calabro's bar: collect examples from **at least five products** that solve the same kind of problem for similar users.

If you are working on a finance app, that means other finance apps your users have — not a design showcase.

If you can't do that simply, you are not ready to claim that a familiar pattern exists.

try.q: How many comparable products does Calabro ask you to find before claiming a pattern is familiar?
options: At least five
At least two
At least ten
One, if it is a market leader
try.explain: Five products solving the same problem for similar users.

test.q: What is Jakob's Law really about?
options: Prevalence across the tools users actually use
Consistency within a single product
The speed at which users learn new patterns
Matching the conventions of your closest competitor

test.q: Which is a valid example of the law?
options: A hamburger icon opening a mobile menu
A custom gesture used in one analytics tool
A novel table interaction that tested poorly
A pattern taken from an award-winning portfolio site
test.explain: Users meet the hamburger daily across hundreds of apps.

test.q: Why should finance app examples come from other finance apps?
options: They are the tools those users actually spend time in
Finance apps have stricter regulatory requirements
Other industries use incompatible design systems
Finance users dislike patterns from consumer apps
test.explain: Prevalence is measured in the user's own environment.

test.q: What is the effect of invoking the law with one screenshot?
options: It ends the discussion without evidence
It satisfies the five-product requirement
It proves the pattern is a usability risk
It shifts the decision to the research team
test.explain: That is the weaponising the title refers to.

test.q: If you can't easily collect comparable examples, what follows?
options: You aren't ready to claim the pattern is familiar
You should test the pattern with five users
You should adopt your competitor's version
The pattern is automatically a bad idea
test.explain: No prevalence, no claim — the pattern may still be fine, but not on these grounds.
